description: We are a bunch of cool CS students and we welcome anyone to join!
summary:
COSMOS 10: Find the Water is an interactive, two-world 3D space mission design game that takes students and aspiring engineers from NASA Kennedy Space Center on Earth (JPL Concept Maturity Levels 1–3) to Shackleton Crater at the Lunar South Pole (CML 4). Players are tasked with a critical Artemis-era directive: locate and harvest subsurface water ice (H2O) inside a pitch-black, -200°C crater while balancing a $450M budget, launch vehicle fairing mass limits, shadow power generation, orbital lifetime, and Deep Space Network (DSN) bandwidth.

Why is it important? Traditional aerospace education teaches rockets, orbits, and instruments in isolated silos. COSMOS 10 bridges this gap by letting players—individually or in a 4-Player Team Role Mode across the 4 NASA Mission Segments (User, Space, Launch, Ground)—build a spacecraft from scratch, experience how every design choice creates real-world engineering trade-offs, launch through a 3D Earth-to-Moon transfer, and operate their custom spacecraft across 4 interactive lunar sectors to earn a NASA Systems Engineering Report Card.
details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

COSMOS 10 is a browser-based, zero-installation Space Mission Design Simulator divided into Two Dimensional Worlds (Earth and The Moon) across 4 progressive stages modeled on NASA JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4):

1. Stage 1 — Mission Concept Definition (CML 1 on Earth):

Players use an interactive physics slingshot at Cape Canaveral to select one of three scientific objectives at the Lunar South Pole:

- Easy (Orbital Surface Frost Mapping): Requires 250W Power | 2 Gbps Data.

- Medium (Crater Ice Spectroscopy): Requires 450W Power | 5 Gbps Data.

- Hard (In-Situ Subsurface Ice Drilling): Requires 650W Power | 7 Gbps Data + Surface Lander & 2m Drill.

2. Stage 2 — Mission Design Lab & Trade Studies (CML 2–3 on Earth):

Starting from an empty launchpad (0/6 slots), players assemble their spacecraft from scratch across the 4 Official NASA Mission Segments:

- Space Segment (Architecture & Hull): Space Orbiter Only ($65M, 240kg), Crater Ice Lander ($110M, 420kg), or Orbiter + Lander Combo ($155M, 600kg).

- User/Science Segment (Stackable Instruments): Players can equip 1, 2, or all 3 NASA instruments—ShadowCam Optical Imager (+100 Sci), NIRVSS Infrared Spectrometer (+250 Sci), and TRIDENT 2m Ice Drill (+500 Sci)—experiencing how adding instruments increases scientific return while driving up mass, power draw, data volume, and cost.

- Space Segment (Power & Thermal): Basic Solar Wings ($30M, freezes in -200°C permanent shadow), Solar + Li-S Mega Battery ($65M), or Nuclear MMRTG Isotope Core ($110M, 24/7 atomic heat & +980W).

- Launch Segment & GMAT Orbit: Light Scout LV (550kg cap), Medium Atlas LV (900kg cap), or Heavy SLS Titan (1,500kg cap), paired with 50km Low Lunar Orbit (12-month lifetime), 90° Polar Orbit (36-month lifetime), or Frozen Elliptical Orbit (60-month lifetime).

- Ground Segment (Communications): Single Ground Station (+2 Gbps, suffers Earth-rotation blackouts) vs. Global 3-Dish Deep Space Network (+5 Gbps, 24/7 coverage).

- Collaboration, Sandbox & Random Events: Includes a 4-Player Team Role Mode (where 4 specialists must negotiate and sign off on their segments), a Sandbox Mode (unlimited constraints for free experimentation), and a Random Constraint Event generator (e.g., Congressional Budget Cuts or Solar Super-Storms).

3. Stage 3 — 3D Launch & Lunar South Pole Operations (CML 4 on the Moon):

Upon ignition, a 3D HTML5 Canvas Earth-to-Moon transfer cutscene transitions the player into the Moon Dimension. The player's Earth hardware directly determines their starting Speed, Shield Durability, and Bonus XP across 4 interactive 3D Hologram Pins on a tilted Shackleton Crater topographic map:

- Pin 1 (Systems Engineering Trade-Off Exam): Interactive assessment teaching the Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation, DSN 120° dish spacing, RTG vs. Solar in shadowed craters, and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).

- Pin 2 (GMAT Orbital Alignment): 10-body solar navigation & gravity alignment puzzle.

- Pin 3 (Crater Ejecta & Micrometeoroid Defense): Real-time HTML5 Canvas laser-ablation deflection simulator where rocket Speed and power Shield HP protect the descending craft.

- Pin 4 (8x8 Hydro-Matrix ISRU Water Extractor): Crystalline block-matrix extraction puzzle to harvest 100 Liters of pure lunar water ice.

4. Stage 4 — Post-Mission Evaluation, Multi-Run Comparison & NASA Archival Proof:

Players receive a 4-Pillar NASA Engineering Report Card (grading Cost Efficiency, Mass Margin, Shadow Power, and Science/Lifetime from A+ to F), a Multi-Run Comparison Table to compare different mission architectures side-by-side, a front-page newspaper dispatch, and real archival photo proof & quotes from NASA’s LCROSS, LRO, SOFIA, and Artemis missions.

Benefits & What We Hope to Achieve

- Transforms abstract systems-engineering math into tactile, visual cause-and-effect that even middle-school, high-school, and university students can grasp immediately.

- Demonstrates that there is no single "perfect" spacecraft—every mission is a trade study between competing priorities.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

- Frontend & Game Engine: 100% Pure Vanilla HTML5, CSS3 (3D Perspective Transforms & Custom Animations), and ES6 JavaScript (zero heavy external frameworks required).

- Graphics & Audio: Interactive SVG live spacecraft assembly, HTML5 2D/3D Canvas particle & arcade physics, and a procedural Web Audio API sound synthesizer (zero external audio files required).

- Hosting: GitHub & GitHub Pages.
